title: Transient Visual Loss: A Clinical & Emergency Masterclass
summary: Transient visual loss (TVL) represents a critical diagnostic challenge necessitating rapid differentiation between benign ocular phenomena and life-threatening neurovascular disease. This guide synthesizes the diagnostic workup for the modern ophthalmologist.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Transient Visual Loss (TVL), or amaurosis fugax, is defined as a monocular or binocular visual deficit lasting seconds to hours with full spontaneous recovery. Incidence increases significantly with age, particularly in patients >60, mirroring the prevalence of carotid artery disease and giant cell arteritis (GCA).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Age >50 with new onset headaches or scalp tenderness (Consider GCA)
Altitudinal or 'curtain coming down' sensation (Suggests carotid source)
Associated motor or sensory deficits (Suggests TIA/Stroke)
Lasting >1 hour without clear migrainous features

sections.title: Clinical Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: History (Duration, laterality, associated symptoms, provoking factors).
Step 2: Full Ophthalmic Exam (Slit lamp, IOP, Funduscopy - look for Hollenhorst plaques).
Step 3: Labs (ESR, CRP, CBC, Platelets, Fasting Glucose, Lipid Panel).
Step 4: Imaging (Carotid Doppler, Echo, CTA/MRA head/neck).
Step 5: Cardiology referral (Holter monitor for occult AFib).

content.explanation: A: Artery (Carotid), B: Blood (Hypercoaguable), C: Cardiac (AFib/Valvular), D: Diabetes/Dyslipidemia, E: ESR/CRP (GCA)

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Hollenhorst plaques are cholesterol emboli (bright, refractive) usually from the ipsilateral carotid artery.
Transient vision loss triggered by postural changes or bright light is pathognomonic for Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (OIS).
Papilledema-associated TVL results from transient elevation of intracranial pressure exceeding perfusion pressure at the optic nerve head.
Always check blood pressure in both arms; asymmetry may indicate subclavian steal syndrome.
